questions.title: Which vitamin deficiency causes pellagra, presenting with dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia?
questions.question: A patient presents with a photosensitive, symmetrical dermatitis over sun-exposed skin, diarrhoea and progressive dementia/confusion. Deficiency of which vitamin produces this classic triad (pellagra)?

explanations.A: Correct. Niacin (vitamin B3, nicotinic acid/nicotinamide) is a precursor of the coenzymes NAD and NADP used throughout cellular energy metabolism. Its deficiency causes pellagra, classically presenting with the triad of the "3 Ds": photosensitive dermatitis in sun-exposed skin, diarrhoea from gastrointestinal mucosal atrophy, and dementia/confusion from CNS energy failure (a 4th D, death, follows if uncorrected). Because niacin can also be synthesised from tryptophan, pellagra can arise from isolated niacin deficiency or from conditions that deplete tryptophan, and it is treated with niacin/nicotinamide replacement.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Thiamine (B1) deficiency causes Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, presenting with a different triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus and ataxia, classically in chronic alcoholics — not pellagra's dermatitis-diarrhoea-dementia picture.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cobalamin (B12) deficiency classically causes subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord and megaloblastic anaemia, not pellagra.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pyridoxine (B6) deficiency classically causes peripheral neuropathy and sideroblastic anaemia, not the pellagra triad.

questions.learning_objective: State that niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency causes pellagra, presenting with the classic triad of dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia.

questions.title: Which metabolite, formed by astrocytic ammonia detoxification, contributes to cerebral oedema in hyperammonaemic encephalopathy?
questions.question: In a patient with a urea cycle defect (or severe liver failure), ammonia accumulates in the blood. Astrocytes detoxify this ammonia using glutamine synthetase, and excess accumulation of the resulting osmotically active product causes astrocyte swelling, contributing to cerebral oedema. Which metabolite is this?

explanations.A: Correct. Astrocytic glutamine synthetase combines the excess ammonia with glutamate to form glutamine, the brain's main route of ammonia detoxification. When ammonia delivery is high and sustained, as in a urea cycle defect or hepatic failure, this drives excessive intra-astrocytic glutamine accumulation; because glutamine is osmotically active, it draws water into the astrocyte, causing astrocyte swelling and cerebral oedema, the core mechanism of hyperammonaemic (hepatic) encephalopathy.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Glutamate is the substrate consumed by glutamine synthetase (combined with ammonia to form glutamine), not the accumulating osmotically active product responsible for astrocyte swelling.
explanations.C: Incorrect. GABA is an inhibitory neurotransmitter synthesised from glutamate by glutamate decarboxylase; it is not part of the astrocytic ammonia-detoxification pathway that drives cerebral oedema here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Urea is the product of the hepatic urea cycle itself, whose impairment is precisely the problem in this scenario; astrocytes do not synthesise urea as their route of ammonia detoxification.

questions.learning_objective: State that in hyperammonaemia from a urea cycle defect, astrocytic conversion of ammonia to glutamine (via glutamine synthetase) causes astrocyte swelling and contributes to cerebral oedema.

questions.title: Which pharmacokinetic property of methadone underlies its use in opioid substitution therapy?
questions.question: Compared with morphine's relatively short elimination half-life, methadone has a much longer half-life. Which clinical consequence of this property is the basis for using methadone as maintenance (substitution) therapy in opioid use disorder?

options.A: Fewer/milder withdrawal symptoms with stable once-daily dosing
options.B: Complete blockade of opioid receptors, preventing any opioid effect
options.C: Rapid reversal of opioid-induced respiratory depression
options.D: A ceiling effect on respiratory depression at high doses

explanations.A: Correct. Methadone's much longer half-life (roughly 15-60 hours) than morphine's produces stable plasma levels with once-daily oral dosing, smoothing out the peaks and troughs in mu-receptor occupancy that drive withdrawal symptoms. This pharmacokinetic property, not any difference in receptor selectivity, is why methadone is used as maintenance (substitution) therapy: it steadily satisfies mu-receptor demand to suppress withdrawal and craving while avoiding the rapid on/off reinforcing effect of shorter-acting opioids such as morphine or heroin.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Complete opioid-receptor blockade without agonist effect describes naltrexone, a pure antagonist used for relapse prevention after detoxification, not methadone, which is itself a full mu-agonist.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Rapid reversal of opioid-induced respiratory depression describes naloxone, a short-acting antagonist used for acute overdose reversal, not methadone's role in maintenance therapy.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A ceiling effect on respiratory depression at high doses is a property of buprenorphine, a partial mu-agonist, not methadone, which is a full agonist without that ceiling.

questions.learning_objective: State that methadone's much longer half-life than morphine's produces fewer/milder withdrawal symptoms, the pharmacokinetic basis for its use in opioid substitution (maintenance) therapy.
